title: Seeing Realism from Simulation: Efficient Video Transfer for Vision-Language-Action Data Augmentation
one_liner: Convert cheap simulated robot videos into realistic looking training videos to teach real robots without collecting expensive real footage.
lead: Robot learning models learn to manipulate objects by watching videos of robots doing tasks. Real videos are expensive to collect but look realistic; simulated videos are free to generate but look fake and cartoon-like. This paper shows how to automatically transform cheap fake-looking simulated videos into realistic-looking ones, keeping the robot actions exactly the same. This lets you train on cheap data that looks real.

problem.h2: Why simulated videos alone are not enough
paras: Robot learning models learn by watching videos of arms, hands, and grippers moving objects around. When you show the model a real-world video of picking up a cup, it sees actual lighting, shadows, wear on materials, clutter, and the specific way objects look under natural light. When you show it a simulated video, the lighting is synthetic, the textures are fake, the background is obviously rendered, and the robot itself looks cartoonish. The model learns these visual differences and expects the real world to look like the simulation. When it sees a real robot, it is shocked by how different things look. This visual mismatch is called domain gap.

Collecting real robot videos is expensive. You need real hardware, human demonstrators, careful labeling, and many hours of footage. Simulation is essentially free: you can generate thousands of videos in parallel on a computer. But because simulated and real videos look so different, models trained only on simulated data fail badly when deployed on actual robots.

callout.html: Collect more and more real robot videos by hand.

steps.text: From each simulated video, extract the objects, their positions, and a text description of what is happening.
Rewrite the caption to describe a different environment (kitchen, lab, office) so the same action appears in variety.
Feed the extracted scene structure and rewritten caption into a video diffusion model (a model that generates video frames from descriptions).
Instead of regenerating every frame from scratch, reuse the internal video representation (tokens) from the previous frame to save time.
The action sequence (hand position over time) stays the same; only the appearance (lighting, textures, surroundings) becomes realistic.

paras: The paper modifies the appearance of simulated videos (colors, lighting, textures, backgrounds) while keeping the robot's movements and object positions frozen. The core change is: replace the synthetic rendering of each frame with a realistic one generated by a video diffusion model (a model that creates videos from descriptions), conditioned on the scene structure.

hidden.h2: The key metric: visual realism aligned with action
hidden.name: domain-gap reduction
paras: The paper measures the visual realism of the generated videos by checking whether a model trained on them transfers to real robots without retraining. This is called zero-shot transfer. A video is useful if it looks real enough that a model trained on it does not get shocked when it sees the real world. The hidden quantity is not explicitly stated in pixels or metrics, but it is the degree to which the generated video matches the statistical pattern of real robot videos in ways that matter for learning.

The paper does not report pixel-level similarity metrics. Instead, it reports robot performance: if a model trained on augmented videos achieves higher success rates on real tasks, the augmentation worked because the visual domain gap shrank.

heat.caption: Darker means more realistic appearance matching real robot videos.

reads.html: A good augmented video has realistic lighting and materials, but the robot's hand stays in the same place, frame by frame, as in the original simulated video.
Visual domain-gap reduction is measured by downstream robot task success. A video is good if a vision-language-action model trained on it generalizes to real robots without task-specific fine-tuning.

mechanism.h2: Why converting simulated videos to realistic ones helps robot learning
paras: A robot-learning model is a pattern detector. When you show it a video of a hand reaching for a cup, it sees pixels: colors, edges, and spatial patterns. It learns associations: hand-at-left + cup-at-right means move-hand-right. If all training videos have synthetic lighting and fake textures, the model learns patterns tied to synthetic images. When you put it on a real robot and show it real video, the lighting is different, the textures are different, and the pixel patterns are not what it learned. The model does not know what to do.

By converting simulated videos to look realistic before training, you change what patterns the model sees. Instead of learning on synthetic images, it learns on images that resemble real video. When deployed, the pixel patterns it sees are closer to what it trained on. The robot actions are still the same simulated actions (so you keep the high-quality labels), but the visual appearance now matches the real world. This is called domain adaptation: you adapt the domain (the appearance) but keep the action labels.

The paper uses a conditional video diffusion model to do this. A diffusion model is a machine that learns to remove noise from images; reversed, it can generate new images from a description. By conditioning it on the extracted scene structure and a rewritten caption, you steer the model to generate videos that (1) have the same objects and spatial layout as the simulated video, (2) have realistic appearance (because the model learned from real video), and (3) still show the same robot actions (because you locked the action coordinates). The 'feature-reuse' trick speeds this up by reusing computation across nearby frames, since consecutive frames differ only slightly.

math.words: A conditional video generation loss is the error between generated video frames and a target description, modified by a guidance weight and a realism classifier. The model learns to generate videos that match the description and look realistic.
symbols: the video frames the diffusion model generates in this step
the target distribution (realistic video style from the training data)
the loss from a realism classifier (how fake the generated video looks)
the weight controlling how much to prioritize realism versus matching the scene structure

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Frame 50 generated: pixel error versus realistic appearance = 0.8; realism loss = 0.3. Total = 0.8 + 1.5 * 0.3 = 1.25.
Frame 51 generated: pixel error = 0.6; realism loss = 0.2. Total = 0.6 + 1.5 * 0.2 = 0.9.
Frame 51 is better because both its pixel match and realism score are lower. Training nudges the model toward frame-51-like outputs.

math.note: The loss guides the diffusion model to generate frames that reconstruct the scene correctly but also look like real video, not simulation.

charts.title: Baseline: simulated data only
charts.note: Training on only simulated video leads to poor real-world performance due to visual domain gap.

charts.title: This paper: augmented realistic videos
charts.note: Converting simulated videos to realistic appearance before training gives consistent improvements across benchmarks. Percentages are illustrative but reflect the 8% and 5.1% gains cited in the paper.

items.b: Generated videos look real but action is wrong.
items.html: If the diffusion model is not carefully conditioned on the action coordinates (hand position, gripper state), it can drift and show a hand at the wrong place, breaking the label.

If you rewrite the caption to a new environment (office instead of kitchen) incorrectly, the diffusion model may generate a scene where the action is no longer valid (trying to pick up a cup from a high shelf instead of a table).

items.b: Augmentation looks real but model does not transfer.
items.html: Visual realism alone is not enough. If the augmented videos do not cover the diversity of real-world lighting, poses, and object types, a model trained on them may still fail when it sees real scenarios that were not represented in the augmentation.

The method works when the diffusion model is tightly conditioned on scene structure and action coordinates, the caption rewriting preserves task validity, and the augmentation includes multiple environments and viewing angles.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small demo that takes a simulated video clip (5-10 frames of a robot arm reaching for an object), extracts the object bounding box and hand coordinates, rewrite the scene description for two different environments, use a conditional video diffusion model (e.g., adapt any open-source video generation model) to synthesize realistic versions with the extracted conditions, and then train a simple vision-language model (a small classifier or regression model) on the real versions and measure whether it correctly predicts hand motion on a held-out real robot video.
demo.metric_eq: Transfer accuracy = real-robot performance with augmented-training / real-robot performance with simulated-only-training
demo.closing: The demo must make visible that the augmented videos look photo-realistic and retain the same action (hand at the same place) while the simulated originals look cartoonish.
